bib.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval, Chapter 8: Evaluation in information retrieval
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition 2009 draft, pp. 151-175)

question: How should an IR system be evaluated: with what test collections, set-based and ranked measures, relevance assessment practice, and user-utility proxies?
contributions: Defines the test-collection model (documents, information needs, binary relevance judgments)
Defines precision, recall, F, interpolated precision, 11-point average, MAP, P@k, R-precision, ROC, NDCG
Covers pooling, kappa agreement, critiques of relevance, A/B testing and result snippets

limits: Written 2008-2009: test collections are TREC/Cranfield/GOV2 (25M pages), tiny by current standards; no mention of neural retrievers, embeddings, LLM judges, MRR, recall@k as used in RAG, or end-to-end answer evaluation
Assumes binary, query-independent relevance; relevance of a document treated as independent of others (authors concede, 8.5.1)
Redundancy/marginal relevance only mentioned, not measured by a given metric
NDCG given with gain 2^R-1 and log2(1+m) discount; no worked numeric example
Exercises have no answers in this PDF
No MRR defined in this chapter
Chapter itself says results from one collection may not transfer across domains or user populations
practices: Use at least about 50 information needs and average over them (8.1, p.152).
Tune parameters on a separate development test collection, report on the test collection (8.1, p.152).
Judge relevance against the information need, not the query words (8.1, p.152).
Do not use accuracy for retrieval; use precision and recall (8.3, p.155).
Combine precision and recall with the harmonic mean (F), choosing beta>1 when recall matters (8.3, p.156).
Use MAP for a single-number summary across recall levels; it weights each information need equally (8.4, pp.159-161).
Use precision at k when only the first page matters, but expect it to be unstable (8.4, p.161).
Use R-precision to adjust for the number of relevant documents (8.4, p.161).
Use NDCG when relevance is graded (8.4, p.163).
Have domain experts design information needs; random query-term combinations are poor (8.5, p.164).
Build judgments by pooling the top k of several systems for large collections (8.5, p.164).
Measure inter-judge agreement with pooled-marginal kappa; average pairwise kappa for more than two judges (8.5, p.166).
Validate offline metrics against live behaviour with single-variable A/B tests on 1-10% of traffic (8.6.3, p.170).
